title: Learning That Lasts: Practice, Timing, and Task
subtitle: Recall practice can beat rereading on delayed memory; useful spacing and guidance depend on the learning goal.

nodes.title: Reread or recall?
nodes.detail: For prose, rereading won after five minutes; recall practice without feedback won after two days or one week.

nodes.title: Space—but not endlessly
nodes.detail: For factual memory, useful gaps grew with the intended retention interval; excessively long gaps reduced performance.

nodes.title: Match practice to the task
nodes.detail: In one small novice troubleshooting study, worked examples alone beat alternating examples and problem-solving after one week.

caveat: These studies tested different tasks. They do not show that rereading is useless, longer gaps always help, or recall practice is best for every learning goal.
illustration: Create ONE panoramic triptych with three equal-sized panels, left to right, corresponding to the three nodes. Cohesive expressive editorial illustration, cream background, teal and coral accents, tactile paper textures, consistent human figures and objects. No words, numbers, written marks, charts, arrows, or symbols resembling letters anywhere. Separate panels with generous cream gutters. LEFT: Compare consulting material with retrieving it. At two adjacent desks, one learner studies an open book containing only a pictorial arrangement of botanical specimens; another has closed the same book and reconstructs its botanical arrangement from memory using specimen tiles. A small immediate view shows the open-book learner's arrangement more complete; a larger later view, distinguished by changed daylight and clothing, shows the recall-practice learner's reconstruction more complete. Use natural scene continuity, not a quantitative score or a universal winner motif. CENTER: Show timing within the same factual-learning activity, not as a rival to retrieval. Two horizontal visual vignettes show a learner studying pictorial specimen cards, returning to them, and later reconstructing the collection. In the upper vignette, a moderate stretch of changing daylight separates the learning sessions and the later reconstruction is fuller. In the lower vignette, a much longer expanse of changing light and seasonal foliage separates sessions, and the later reconstruction has missing specimens. Make elapsed time concrete through environmental changes, without calendars, clocks, or written notation. RIGHT: Show two novice learners working on identical simple electrical training boards with physical wires, bulbs, switches, and connectors. One follows a sequence of detailed pictorial worked examples; the other alternates looking at examples with attempting the board independently. In a later inset integrated into the same panel, the examples-only learner has a more successfully assembled board. Keep the comparison modest and specific to this workshop task, without trophies, failure caricatures, or any suggestion that independent practice is universally harmful.
